etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English primitif, from Old French primitif, from Latin prīmitīvus (“first or earliest of its kind”), from prīmus (“first”); see prime. Doublet of primitivo.

definitions.definition: (linguistics) An original or primary word; a word not derived from another, as opposed to derivative.
A member of a primitive society.
(programming) A data type that is built into the programming language, as opposed to more complex structures.
(programming) Any of the simplest elements (instructions, statements, etc.) available in a programming language.[1]

quote.citation: 2021, Arti Noor, Abhijit Sen, Gaurav Trivedi, Proceedings of Emerging Trends and Technologies on Intelligent Systems: ETTIS 2021, page 26:
quote.text: A write-what-where primitive allows the attacker to write arbitrary data wherever they want in the memory

definitions.definition: A basic geometric shape from which more complex shapes can be constructed.
(mathematics) A function whose derivative is a given function; an antiderivative.
Of or pertaining to the beginning or origin, or to early times; original; primordial; primeval; first.

quote.citation: 1895, Edmund Montgomery, “To Be Alive, What is it?”, in The Monist:
quote.text: it is from such primitive beings that the highest organisms now extant are the marvellously developed descendants

definitions.definition: Relating to an art style characterized by asymmetrical shapes and faded colors.
Of or pertaining to or harking back to a former time; old-fashioned; characterized by simplicity.

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 4, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: By some paradoxical evolution rancour and intolerance have been established in the vanguard of primitive Christianity. Mrs. Spoker, in common with many of the stricter disciples of righteousness, was as inclement in demeanour as she was cadaverous in aspect.

quote.citation: 1951 August, “The Why and the Wherefore: The West Sussex Railway”, in Railway Magazine, page 573:
quote.text: The intermediate stations were of the most primitive type.

quote.citation: 1959, Mircea Eliade, “Introduction”, in Willard R. Trask, transl., The Sacred and the Profane: The Nature of Religion (Harvest Book; HB 144), New York, N.Y.: Harcourt, Brace & World, →ISBN, page 11:
quote.text: It could be said that the history of religions—from the most primitive to the most highly developed—is constituted by a great number of hierophanies, by manifestations of sacred realities.

quote.citation: 1831, Noah Webster, Rudiments of English Grammar; Being an Abridgment of the Improved Grammar of the English Language, New-Haven, page 6:
quote.text: Division of words. Words are primitive or radical, and derivative or compound.Of primitive words. Primitive or radical words are such as cannot be divided, or separated into parts which are significant; as man, hope, bless.

definitions.definition: (biology) Occurring in or characteristic of an early stage of development or evolution.
(mathematics) Not derived from another of the same type
(linguistics, dated) most recent common ancestor (often hypothetical) of

quote.citation: 1933, Leonard Bloomfield, Language, Henry Holt, page 13:
quote.text: We infer that other groups of related languages, such as the Germanic (or the Slavic or the Celtic), which show a similar resemblance, have arisen in the same way; it is only an accident of history that for these groups we have no written records of the earlier state of the language, as it was spoken before the differentiation set in. To these unrecorded languages we give names like Primitive Germanic (Primitive Slavic, Primitive Celtic, and so on).
